abstract: Macromolecular crowding shapes biochemical reactions in subtle ways, yet a general framework connecting enzyme activity to the physical properties of polymeric crowders remains elusive. Here we show that polymer scaling concepts provide a common framework to organize the effects of crowding on enzyme activity. Using dextran as a model crowder and fluorescence measurements extending beyond the initial-rate regime, we measure the time course of product formation upon peptide hydrolysis by a representative protease. Time-dependent analysis with a reversible kinetic model yields an inferred equilibrium constant whose dependence on dextran concentration collapses onto a common exponential curve after rescaling by a molecular-weight-dependent concentration. We show that the latter displays the same scaling law as the overlap concentration expected for branched dextran, linking quantitatively the reaction response to a fundamental property of polymer solutions. The common behaviour breaks down for the largest dextran at concentrations well above this scale, identifying the limits of the common scaling behaviour. Altogether, these findings suggest that polymer overlap is a general organizing principle for interpreting biochemical kinetics in polymer-crowded solutions.
